title: Question 10
stem: Ultrasound and X-rays are both types of wave that are used in medical diagnosis to form images of internal body structures.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Complete Table 10.1 to state, for each type of wave:

• the method of production of the wave
• whether the wave that is detected and used to form the image is the wave that has been absorbed, reflected or transmitted by the internal body structure.

Table 10.1

markscheme_points.text: X-ray production: electrons hitting metal target

hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about the nature of each wave - ultrasound is a high-frequency sound vibration, while X-rays are high-energy electromagnetic waves. What kind of device could make each type vibrate or radiate?

Hint 2: For ultrasound, recall the special crystal in the probe that changes shape when a voltage is applied and produces a voltage when it is squeezed. For X-rays, recall what happens inside the vacuum tube when fast electrons are suddenly stopped.
Hint 3: Now think about how the image is formed - does the probe listen for echoes coming back, or does a detector on the other side of the body measure what gets through?

Hint 4: Match the words reflected and transmitted to the correct imaging method - pulse-echo relies on boundaries sending waves back, while shadow imaging relies on different absorption along the path.
parts.proper_answer: ultrasound method of production: vibrating quartz / piezoelectric crystal (transducer); X-ray method of production: high-speed electrons hitting a metal target; ultrasound detected wave: reflected; X-ray detected wave: transmitted.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **How Ultrasound Is Made**
Think of ultrasound as sound above $20\text{ kHz}$ that must be made to vibrate mechanically. Inside the probe is a quartz crystal that shows the piezoelectric effect. When an alternating voltage is applied it vibrates at ultrasonic frequency and emits an ultrasound pulse.

Step 2: **How X-rays Are Made**
Think of X-rays as photons produced when energetic electrons lose energy very suddenly. In an X-ray tube, electrons are accelerated in vacuum and collide with a rotating metal target. Their rapid deceleration and atomic transitions emit X-ray photons.

Step 3: **What Is Detected For Each Image**
For ultrasound scanning, the same probe acts as receiver. Pulses travel into the body and are partly reflected at boundaries between different tissues. The reflected echo is detected and its time delay gives depth information.
For X-ray imaging, the beam passes right through the body onto film or a detector on the opposite side. Denser tissue like bone absorbs more, so the detected wave is the transmitted wave that has survived passage through the body.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text:
For one type of wave passing through tissue, the wave has $72\%$ of its initial intensity after it has passed through $6.2\text{ cm}$ of the tissue.

Calculate the linear attenuation coefficient $\mu$ of the tissue for this wave.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on what is happening to intensity - it does not fall linearly, it falls by a fixed fraction per cm. Note that $I/I_0 = 0.72$ after $x = 6.2\text{ cm}$ and think about which exponential law links $I$, $I_0$, $\mu$ and $x$.
Hint 2: Take natural logs of both sides to make $\mu$ the subject, keeping $x$ in cm so that $\mu$ comes out in $\text{cm}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **The Law Governing Loss Of Intensity**
When a narrow beam passes through uniform tissue, intensity is lost exponentially because each thin slice removes the same fraction. You can write this as $$I = I_0 \exp(-\mu x)$$ where $I_0$ is initial intensity, $I$ is intensity after thickness $x$, and $\mu$ is the linear attenuation coefficient.

Step 2: **Put In The Numbers And Solve For Mu**
Here $I/I_0 = 0.72$ and $x = 6.2\text{ cm}$. So $$0.72 = \exp(-\mu \times 6.2)$$ Take natural logs: $$\ln(0.72) = -\mu \times 6.2$$ $$\mu = -\frac{\ln(0.72)}{6.2} = 0.053\text{ cm}^{-1}$$ The negative sign disappears because $\ln(0.72)$ is negative, leaving a positive $\mu$ to 2 s.f.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
Another wave of the same type as in (b)(i) passes through $9.3\text{ cm}$ of the same tissue.

Calculate the percentage of the initial intensity of the wave that is attenuated by the tissue.
hints: Hint 1: Remember that attenuated means removed from the beam, not what is left. First work out the fraction that is transmitted through the new thickness of $9.3\text{ cm}$ using your value of $\mu$.
Hint 2: Convert the transmitted fraction to a percentage loss by subtracting from 1 (or 100%) to find what has been attenuated.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find The Transmitted Fraction**
Use the same law with the same $\mu = 0.053\text{ cm}^{-1}$ but new thickness $x = 9.3\text{ cm}$: $$\frac{I}{I_0} = \exp(-\mu x) = \exp(-0.053 \times 9.3)$$ $$\frac{I}{I_0} \approx 0.61$$ So about 61% gets through.

Step 2: **Convert To Percentage Attenuated**
Attenuated means absorbed or scattered out of the beam, so it is what does NOT get through: $$\text{fraction attenuated} = 1 - \frac{I}{I_0} = 1 - 0.61 = 0.39$$ $$\text{percentage attenuated} = 0.39 \times 100\% = 39\%$$
